rv.q: Grammer, touchingly, and blessedly, relaxes on it, stopping well short of the full Shirley Bassey.
So, despite the starry casting of this really patchy production – it is odd watching Kelsey Grammer and Nicholas Lyndhurst side by side...what sustains most interest is simply the curiosity factor.
This creaking, effortful production, mounted in collaboration with English National Opera, doesn't help.

Here all the stops are pulled out but, despite the commitment of the ENO orchestra, the result is a misfire. It says much that only a giant staircase, constantly lowered in James Noone’s metallic design, was moving.
Grammer, though, kinda gets the last laugh, earns his spurs.

Producers Michael Linnit and Michael Grade don’t make a convincing case for reviving it: a mismatched celebrity cast and a by-numbers production mean that contemporary relevance, like chivalry, really is an impossible dream.
Some of its directorial choices are contradictory and superfluous but overall Man of La Mancha is really good fun.
Man of La Mancha hasn't been performed professionally in London since 1968. It can now return to the museum.
But, overall, this is really only one for the musical theatre completists.
An agreeable enough star turn from Kelsey Grammer in an otherwise disappointing evening.
A lumbering show has its moments of familiarity as “The Impossible Dream” pops up again (and again), but mostly the dream that's impossible is to make it feel alive and relevant today.

cn.t: Critics find this rare revival of the 1965 musical charmless and dated, with most questioning why it hasn't been seen in London for 50 years. Grammer's performance disappoints, though "The Impossible Dream" remains an earworm.
